newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Funds seen lifting copper on Chile strike threat.
newsitem.headline: Funds seen lifting copper on Chile strike threat.

text.p: Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are seen opening strongly later on Friday on news Chilean state copper workers may go on strike over government plans to privatise state companies, dealers said.

The strike threat emerged after the LME closed on Thursday and funds could seize on the news to continue a speculative rally that on Thursday saw copper touch a year high of $2,475 a tonne, -- the highest level since before the Sumitomo debacle.
"It will certainly underpin the market. People will use this to push the spreads further," a senior dealer for a European metal trading company said.

On Thursday, union leaders for Chilean state copper workers said they were considering calling strike action to protest at the government's reported plans to privatise parts of the state oil company Enap and state metals smelting firm Enami.

The Confederation of Copper Workers, which claims 17,000 members, agreed with union leaders from Enap (Empresa Nacional del Petroleo) and Enami (Empresa Nacional de Mineria) to coordinate protest actions in case the government announces any privatisations, they said.

LME brokers Brandeis said in its daily review that the bullish close on Thursday, when three month copper was last indicated at $2,473/78 a tonne, will allow the red metal to target $2,630 over the next few weeks.
Three-month copper was quoted by regional dealers at 0300 GMT at $2,472/77 a tonne.
"The Chilean news will be used by the funds to really push the market," another dealer for a foreign metal trading house said. "The question is how long they can sustain this."
Far East dealers said concerns over supply shortages due to power rationing caused by a drought in Chile and the rumblings of labour problems will provide a bullish backdrop for copper.
The premium of cash over three month metal in Asian trade was seen between $95-$105 against a level of $110 on the LME, dealers said.
Zinc prices were also expected to move higher although the upside may be limited after the metal climbed to a 4-1/2 year high on the LME on Thursday at $1,358 a tonne, dealers said.
"There's still some room on the upside for zinc," one said.

Brandeis said, however, that zinc closed poorly on the charts. "A new base needs to form in the $1,340/50 range before fresh gains can be made. The next target on the upside is $1,400, with support seen at $1,330," it said.
